## Learning Objectives

1. Describe the \alert{sampling distribution} of an estimate $\checkmark$
2. Describe how the size and bias of a sample affects the \alert{sampling distribution} $\checkmark$ (li\`ili\`i bit more)
3. Calculate the \alert{standard error of the mean} $\checkmark$
4. Calculate \alert{confidence intervals} using the \alert{standard error of the mean}
5. Know how to correctly interpret \alert{confidence intervals}
6. Display and correctly interpret \alert{error bars} on a graph

## Review of \alert{standard error} and \alert{sampling distribution}

If we went out again and collected a different sample of 20 individuals (*many* **many** times) would we get roughly the same estimate or not? **SE tells us!**

- The wider the sampling distribution, the bigger the SE
- (The SE is the SD of the sampling distribution)
- The bigger the SE, the less likely we are to get similar estimates across repeated samples
- The less likely we are to get similar estimates across samples, the less \alert{confident} we are in the accuracy of any one sample


# Why do we care?

We collect a sample of \alert{$n = 20$} measurements, here it is:

```
35.16, 23.81, 32.65, 22.94, 32.35, 
33.57, 37.94, 33.08, 22.13, 32.05, 
25.24, 36.67, 28.64, 33.49, 27.11, 
27.55, 26.89, 37.60, 34.26, 27.82
```

The mean is `30.548` cm

\Large
But the *historic* mean length of uhu was 42 cm.  So do our data give us confidence they are really smaller today?  

# Confidence Intervals 

## 4. Calculate \alert{confidence intervals} using the \alert{standard error of the mean}

Note: We can calculate CIs for any parameter, but for now we'll focus on the CIs of the mean

## 4. Calculate \alert{confidence intervals} using the \alert{standard error of the mean}

Recall that the mean $\pm$ 2 standard deviations covers roughly 95% of the probability of different values

```{r, fig.width=3, fig.height=2.5, fig.align='center'}
library(socorro)

par(mar = c(2, 1, 2, 0) + 0.5)
denFill(rnorm(10000000), main = "mean = 0, sd = 1", xlim = c(-4, 4), yaxt = "n")
mtext("Probability density", 2)
text(0, 0.1, "95% of\nprobability")
```


## 4. Calculate \alert{confidence intervals} using the \alert{standard error of the mean}


The \alert{confidence interval} is a range of values surrounding the sample estimate that is
likely to contain the true population parameter

\Large
It is simply the mean $\pm$ 2 \alert{standard errors}


## Are uhu smaller now than in the past?

```{r, fig.align='center', fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
x <- c(35.16, 23.81, 32.65, 22.94, 32.35, 
       33.57, 37.94, 33.08, 22.13, 32.05, 
       25.24, 36.67, 28.64, 33.49, 27.11, 
       27.55, 26.89, 37.60, 34.26, 27.82)


se_x <- sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)) 
lower_ci <- mean(x) - 2 * se_x
upper_ci <- mean(x) + 2 * se_x

colz <- viridis::viridis(3)[2]

ggplot() +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower_ci, xmax = upper_ci, y = 1), 
                   height = 0.1, color = colz) +
    geom_point(aes(x = mean(x), y = 1), size = 3, color = colz) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 42, size = 1, color = colz) + 
    theme_cowplot() +
    labs(x = "Uhu, mean length (cm)", y = "") + 
    xlim(lower_ci - 10, 42 + 10) +
    ylim(0.5, 1.5) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), 
          axis.ticks.y = element_blank(), 
          axis.line.y = element_blank()) +
    annotate("text", x = mean(x), y = 1.05, label = "present mean and 95% CI", 
             hjust = 0.5, vjust = -0.5) + 
    annotate("text", x = 42, y = 1.05, label = "historic mean", 
             hjust = -0.1, vjust = -0.5) 

```


## Confidence interval of the mean

Imagine a single sample with mean $\bar{Y}$ collected from a population 

The population has a true mean value $\mu$

The 95% confidence interval for the mean is $\bar{Y} \pm 2 \times \text{SE}$

95% of the time, the 95% confidence interval will overlap the true (but unknown) population mean

## Confidence interval of the mean

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="50%"}

df <- tibble(
  x = 0.1,
  y = 0,
  ymin = 0, ymax = 0,
  xmin = -0.9, xmax = 1.1
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 10) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax), height = 0,
                 show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
  annotate("text", -0.9, 0, label = "lower\nlimit", vjust = -0.25, size = 18) +
  annotate("text", 1.1, 0, label = "upper\nlimit", vjust = -0.25, size = 18) +
  annotate("text", 0.1, 0, label = expression(italic(bar(Y))), vjust = -0.5, size = 18) +
  annotate("label", 0, 0.05, label = expression(mu), size = 18) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.5, 1.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.1, 0.1)) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )

```

## Confidence interval of the mean

Sometimes the confidence interval will not include the population parameter

The confidence interval in red does not include $\mu$

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="50%"}

df <- tibble(
  x = c(0.1, 1.1),
  y = c(-0.5, 0.5),
  ymin = y, ymax = y,
  xmin = x - 1, xmax = x + 1,
  color = LETTERS[1:2]
)

ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = color)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "red")) +
  geom_point(size = 10, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax), height = 0,
                 show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
  annotate("label", 0, 0.05, label = expression(mu), size = 18) +
  theme_cowplot() +
  # scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.5, 1.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )

```




## 95% confidence intervals

On average, 19 of 20 CIs will include the population parameter

```{r, fig.align="center", out.height="70%", warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

ci_rand <- function(nrep, size, bias = 0, seed = 123) {
    mu <- 0
    sig <- 1
    
    set.seed(seed)
    
    # draw ybar from sampling dist
    ybar <- rnorm(nrep, mu, sig / sqrt(size))
    
    # sd^2 * (n-1) is chisq distrib with df n - 1, so se is this...
    se <- sqrt(rchisq(nrep, size - 1) / (size - 1) / size)
    
    lwr <- ybar - 2 * se + bias
    upr <- ybar + 2 * se + bias
    
    res <- data.frame(ybar = ybar + bias, 
                      se = se,
                      lwr = lwr,
                      upr = upr,
                      overlap = lwr <= mu & upr >= mu,
                      r = rank(ybar))
    
    return(res)
}


ci_show <- function(df) {
    ggplot(df, aes(ybar, r, color = overlap)) +
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
        geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), height = 0,
                       show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
        scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black")) +
        geom_point(show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
        theme_cowplot() +
        theme(
            axis.title = element_blank(),
            axis.text = element_blank(),
            axis.line.y = element_blank(),
            axis.ticks = element_blank()
        )
}
```

## Different levels of confidence

95% Confidence Intervals ara a common choice, but we could choose any percent

\begin{alertblock}{Pause \& Think}

Will 90\% confidence intervals be wider or narrower than 95\% confidence intervals?
  
\end{alertblock}


## 90% CIs are narrower than 95% CIs

18 of 20 CIs include the population parameter

Less stringent CIs are narrower because they do not have to include the population parameter as often

```{r, fig.align="center", out.height="70%"}
df1 <- mutate(df, lwr = ybar - 1.8 * se, upr = ybar + 1.8 * se) |>
    mutate(overlap = (lwr <= 0 & upr >= 0))

ci_show(df1)
```




## Bias shifts the sampling distribution

* If your sample is biased, increasing sample size doesn't help
* Because of increased precision, you're estimate is probably farther from the population parameter


## Bias shifts the sampling distribution

Confidence intervals from biased samples will include the population parameter less often

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="60%"}

df$bias <- "Unbiased"
df2 <- ci_rand(20, 10, 0.75, 868239)
df2$bias <- "Biased"

df3 <- rbind(df, df2)

ggplot(df3, aes(ybar, r, color = overlap)) +
    facet_grid(cols = vars(bias)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), height = 0,
                   show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black")) +
    geom_point(show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.line.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 24)
    )

```


## Pseudoreplication leads to overconfidence

Pseudoreplication occurs when two sampled units are not independent

* Multiple measurements from the same patient 
* Genetic variation of related individuals
* Species within the same genus

Usually, this leads to overconfidence because we've underestimated the spread of the sampling distribution

Pseudoreplication can occur with or without bias

## Pseudoreplication leads to overconfidence

With pseudoreplication, our CIs are too narrow, meaning **overconfident**. That overconfidence leads to failing to include the population parameter more often

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="60%"}

df$random <- "All independent"
df4 <- mutate(df, lwr = ybar - 1 * se, upr = ybar + 1 * se) |>
    mutate(overlap = (lwr <= 0 & upr >= 0))
df4$random <- "Pseudoreplicated"

df4 <- rbind(df, df4)

ggplot(df4, aes(ybar, r, color = overlap)) +
    facet_grid(cols = vars(random)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), height = 0,
                   show.legend = FALSE, size = 2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black")) +
    geom_point(show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.line.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 24)
    )

```

## \alert{Error bars}

- Standard error of the mean or CIs are most common
- Clearly label if error bars are $\pm$ 1 SE, 2 SE, $s$, etc.
- Think carefully about what you are trying to *show* 


## \alert{Error bars}

- Think carefully about what you are trying to *show* 

If the spread of the data, show standard deviation (or just use a box plot which shows inner quartile range)

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=5.5, fig.height=2.5}
set.seed(123)
dat <- data.frame(group = rep(LETTERS[1:2], 20), 
                  y = rnorm(40))
dat$y[dat$group == "B"] <- dat$y[dat$group == "B"] + 2

gd1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = group, y = y, color = group)) + 
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    ggtitle("Data with\nSD error bars") +
    stat_summary(fun = mean,
                 fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x),
                 fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x),
                 geom = "errorbar",
                 width = 0.2,
                 size = 1)

gd2 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = group, y = y, color = group)) + 
    geom_boxplot() +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none") +
    ggtitle("Boxplot")
    

plot_grid(gd1, gd2)
```


## \alert{Error bars}

- Think carefully about what you are trying to *show* 

If the estimate of the mean and its uncertainty, show standard error or confidence intervals

```{r fig.align='center', fig.width=5.5, fig.height=2.5}

gm <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = group, y = y, color = group)) + 
    geom_jitter(width = 0.1, color = "gray") +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

gm1 <- gm + 
    ggtitle("Mean with\nSE error bars") +
    stat_summary(fun = mean,
                 fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),
                 fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),
                 geom = "errorbar",
                 width = 0.2,
                 size = 1)

gm2 <- gm + 
    ggtitle("Mean with\n95% CI error bars") +
    stat_summary(fun = mean,
                 fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - 2 * sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),
                 fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + 2 * sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),
                 geom = "errorbar",
                 width = 0.2,
                 size = 1)

plot_grid(gm1, gm2)
```
